pages.x: When Japan surrendered in 1945, Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam independent before a vast crowd in Hanoi, quoting the American Declaration of Independence. But France wanted its colony back. Its troops returned to the south, and in March 1946 they landed in the north, under a deal with Ho that soon fell apart.

In November 1946 a quarrel over customs in the port of Haiphong turned into fighting, and French warships shelled the city. In December the Viet Minh attacked the French in Hanoi, and Ho Chi Minh and his government slipped away to the hills of the north to fight.
pages.of: killed when French guns shelled Haiphong

pages.x: The Viet Minh army was led by Võ Nguyên Giáp, a former history teacher with no military training, who admired Napoleon. He began with small bands fighting a guerrilla war in the jungle, and in 1947 Ho Chi Minh barely escaped when French paratroopers dropped on the Viet Minh headquarters.

In 1949 the communists won in China, and the Viet Minh suddenly had a friendly country at their back, with weapons, training and advisers. In 1950 Giáp's new regular divisions destroyed the French columns on Route 4 near the Chinese border, at Cao Bằng, France's worst colonial defeat in almost two centuries.

The war now looked like part of the Cold War, and the United States began to pay for it: by 1954 it was meeting most of the cost. A new French commander, General de Lattre, ringed the Red River Delta with concrete forts, and in 1951 he beat back Giáp's attacks on it.

In late 1953 the French dropped paratroopers into the valley of Dien Bien Phu, near Laos, and built a fortress to lure Giáp into battle. Giáp accepted. His men hauled guns over the mountains by hand, and supplies on bicycles, and from March 1954 their artillery, hidden on the hills, shut the airstrip and took the strongpoints one by one.

After almost two months of siege, on 7 May 1954, the fortress fell. About 11,000 French and colonial soldiers were marched away as prisoners, and fewer than a third came back alive. The next day, at a conference in Geneva, the talks on Indochina began.
pages.of: French and colonial troops taken prisoner

pages.x: At Geneva in July France agreed to leave. Vietnam was split for the time being at the 17th parallel, the communists taking the north and a government friendly to the West the south, with elections promised for 1956 to unite the country. Laos and Cambodia became independent. The elections were never held.

The French empire in Asia was over, and that same year France was drawn into another colonial war, in Algeria. In Vietnam the line drawn at Geneva hardened into a border, and as the United States took France's place in the south, the country slid toward a second, even longer war.
pts: France fought to take back its colony
The Viet Minh won at Dien Bien Phu
Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel
